Karin Loh began her doctorate in October 2017 at the Institute for Hearing Technology and Acoustics (IHTA) at RWTH Aachen University. Her deceptively simple question, whether children hear differently from adults, draws on auditory selective attention, child psychology and educational acoustics. Loh studied electrical engineering with a focus on computer engineering; a bachelor’s thesis at the Institute of Technical Acoustics (ITA, now IHTA) on acoustic and visual cues in an auditory selective attention paradigm drew her in.

Her projects covered noise exposure in daycare centers, kindergartens and primary schools, funded by the HEAD-Genuit Foundation and measured with child-appropriate methods; a paradigm for children’s selective attention, developed with a postdoc at RWTH’s Institute of Psychology; further work funded by RWTH’s Exploratory Research Space (ERS), which backs risky interdisciplinary ideas; and the EU Horizon 2020 project Equal-Life, on how genetic, psychological and environmental factors together shape children’s health and development.

A doctorate at RWTH takes five to six years on average. Doctoral researchers are employed as research associates, teach, and supervise theses and exercises, building professional, methodological, communication and social skills. Her supervisor, Professor Janina Fels, encouraged her to attend DAGA, the German acoustics conference, and international meetings from her first year. Loh is active in the Young Acousticians Network, mentoring programs, DEGA’s hearing acoustics group and an EAA technical committee. Appointed Oberingenieurin (senior engineer) in her fourth year, she gained grant-writing experience; she is now weighing academic and industry careers.

Adapted into Chinese by Fanyu Meng from Karin Loh’s first-person profile in Akustik Journal, published by the German Acoustical Society (DEGA).
